intro: Catch up on the key A Level ideas. Complete four retrieval questions, work through the examples, then practise and explain your reasoning.

blocks.title: Knowledge before judgement
blocks.text: An alert is an estimate, not proof. False positives flag harmless activity; false negatives miss genuine concerns. Overall accuracy can hide different error rates for different groups.

blocks.title: Privacy and fairness
blocks.text: Monitoring can reveal sensitive activity. Limit collection and access to what the purpose requires. Biased training data or poor context can make particular groups more likely to be flagged unfairly.

blocks.title: People and work
blocks.text: Automating the first scan could save staff time. Checking alerts, training and appeals also require time and skills. Work may shift towards review rather than simply disappear.

blocks.title: Develop the reasoning
blocks.text: Name a stakeholder, explain the mechanism, then show a consequence. “It saves time” is a point; “staff can review a concern sooner, so a pupil may receive earlier support” develops it.

blocks.title: Worked example · Point
blocks.text: Pupils could benefit from earlier safeguarding support. Name who benefits and the specific benefit; “AI is useful” would be too vague.

blocks.title: Worked example · Explain
blocks.text: The system could flag concerning activity sooner than staff manually reviewing the same activity. Give a plausible mechanism. “Could” recognises that this benefit needs evidence rather than being guaranteed.

blocks.title: Choose a relevant point
blocks.text: A. Keeping every history could intrude on pupils’ privacy. B. Keeping every history must make pupils feel safer.

blocks.title: Stronger choice: A
blocks.text: Keeping every browsing history could intrude on pupils’ privacy. A identifies a plausible risk. B assumes that all pupils will feel safer without evidence.

blocks.title: Choose an explanation
blocks.text: A. Privacy matters because privacy is important to pupils. B. A full history could reveal sensitive interests beyond a concern.

blocks.title: Stronger choice: B
blocks.text: Full histories could reveal sensitive interests beyond a particular safeguarding concern. B explains what creates the risk. A repeats the point without explaining it.

questions.feedback: ONE POSSIBLE DEVELOPED ANSWER Automatic detention could reduce the time staff spend deciding initial sanctions. However, legitimate research could trigger a false alert, so a pupil may be punished unfairly and lose trust before an appeal is heard. I would reject automatic detention on an alert alone: review before action matters more than this time saving. A later appeal does not undo all of the initial harm. Check: explain both effects, weigh their importance and judge this change. Other supported conclusions are possible; an alert alone is not proof.

However, past hiring decisions may contain bias, and career breaks do not establish a lack of skill. Rejecting these applicants without review could exclude capable people unfairly. I would not approve this design: the speed benefit does not justify an unexplained exclusion. Assess job-relevant evidence, audit outcomes and offer meaningful human review before relying on it. Check: transfer the reasoning to recruitment; develop effects on both groups; justify a decision. “AI is biased” alone…
